title: New Oregon revenue forecast predicts $245M more than expected for next budget cycle
summary: The November forecast expects about $245M more than previously expected in the upcoming budget cycle. The article also gives about $233M more for 2027-29 and about $11M more for the current two-year budget, without saying how the figures relate. Gains come largely from higher-income Oregonians, and state economists cautioned that such booms tend to correct. Business taxes are expected to run about $71M over projections; the article says that money funds schools instead of being returned to corporations. The forecast comes with Kotek facing a Dec 1 deadline for her budget.
key_facts: ~$245M more than previously expected for the upcoming budget cycle
~$11M more for the current two-year budget
business taxes expected ~$71M above projections; that money would go to schools
note: Checked against the article 2026-11-21. Its $233M and $245M match OEA Table B.1b: net General Fund revenue up $233.5M and available resources up $244.6M for 2027-29, the difference being an $11.2M larger beginning balance [SRC:fiscal/oea/2026-12_forecast.pdf p.63].

title: Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek unveils policy proposals for a second term
summary: Kotek's reelection platform, "Building Oregon's Future Together," has four parts: affordability, the economy, improving K-12 schools, and defending what makes Oregon distinct. For schools it would raise classroom time to the national average by the end of a second term, which the article notes could be costly, reduce student absences, strengthen diploma requirements and limit social media on school-issued devices. Universal preschool is listed under affordability. The article says the plan doesn't detail how its initiatives would be paid for or pursued. It does not mention the school funding formula or enrollment-based funding.
key_facts: Byline dated Sept. 18, 2026, 12:20 a.m.; URL and page metadata say Sept. 17
Instructional time to the national average by end of second term
No mention of enrollment-based funding or the formula (checked Nov. 22, 2026, #114)
note: Summary rewritten Nov. 22, 2026 against the article (#114). The earlier summary, carried over from a research brief, listed literacy, chronic absenteeism and revisiting enrollment-based funding, which the article doesn't mention.

title: Powerful Lawmakers Say They Don't Anticipate Tapping Education Stability Fund This Year
summary: At a May 7 school funding forum hosted by Community + Parents for Public Schools, Ways and Means co-chairs Sen. Kate Lieber and Rep. Tawna Sanchez said they saw no reason to tap the Education Stability Fund this year. Lieber said the Legislature might have looked to the fund in the short session had it been forced to cut school funding below the current service level, and warned that one-time money for ongoing costs leaves a cliff. Sanchez said worse years are coming as federal H.R. 1 shifts social-service costs to the state in 2027-29 and 2029-31, stressed her interest in revenue reform, and cautioned against relying on one-time dollars.

title: Cashing In on Oregon School Kids
summary: An OJP investigation (by James Neff, part of its "Oregon Schools: What Went Wrong" series) examines Oregon's online schools, many operated by for-profit firms (Stride, Connections Academy, OpenEd among them), and reports that their graduation rates trail the state's while ODE's oversight has been thin. Because state school money follows each enrolled student, small rural districts that sponsor or run statewide online programs collect funding for students who live elsewhere; the article's main example is Nyssa, whose online program enrolls more students than its brick-and-mortar schools and which kept a share of the per-student money under its contract with OpenEd. It also covers parent stipends paid by some programs, a 2017 Secretary of State audit and 2019 follow-up that found ODE had not fully carried out its recommendations, and parents who say online school works for their families. Kotek said in a statement to OJP that she is reviewing the state's approach; her November opponent did not respond.
key_facts: About 31,000 students, roughly 6% of K-12, are in the state's online programs (all online programs, not only virtual charters)
Oregon has 76 virtual schools, per the article

Nyssa's contract gave OpenEd 60% of per-student funding and Nyssa kept 40%; article puts Nyssa's share at about $4,650 per online student, or $14 million (a later passage refers to $12 million in public funds spent on the virtual school)
Article says each student who leaves a brick-and-mortar school for a virtual one costs that school more than $11,000
Article names no 2025 or 2026 bills and does not mention ORS 338 or the 3% enrollment rule

title: As Oregon students lag, lawmakers may consider sweeping review of education agency
summary: Rep. Hai Pham (D-Hillsboro) is backing an external management review of the Oregon Department of Education for the 2027 session, comparing its size, structure and duties with agencies in states with better results. The article contrasts ODE's staffing with Washington's OSPI. ODE Director Charlene Williams attributes the difference to the number of grant programs and legislative mandates ODE administers, and says streamlining is underway. It cites Urban Institute's demographically adjusted NAEP results and NEA spending figures, and notes ODOT's 2025 external review as a precedent.
key_facts: Washington OSPI ~300 employees; 295 districts; ~1.05 million students
Urban Institute (adjusted for income and demographics): Oregon elementary and middle schoolers scored lower than nearly every other state on 2024 NAEP reading and math
Oregon spends slightly above the national average per student (NEA figures)
At least 300 education bills expected in the 2027 session, which begins Jan. 19

title: Julie Fahey is out as Oregon House speaker
summary: In a closed-door caucus vote on Friday evening, Nov 20, House Democrats declined to back Speaker Julie Fahey for another term and chose Majority Leader Ben Bowman as their nominee for speaker. With Democrats holding 39 of 60 seats, OPB says he is nearly certain to win the full House vote in January. Bowman has worked as a school administrator and once chaired the Tigard-Tualatin School Board. The article notes that speakers decide committee assignments.
